title: Selecting Mesh Faces by Position and Normal in ANSYS Mechanical
text:
For a moving heat-source model, I needed to select mesh faces near a point and facing a specified direction. The script below does this in two filters: it finds nearby element centroids, then checks the orientation of each candidate face.


For an xy search, an element with centroid \(\mathbf{c}\) is retained when
\[
(c_x-q_x)^2+(c_y-q_y)^2 \le r^2,
\]
where \(\mathbf{q}\) is the search center and \(r\) is the radius. Ignoring the third coordinate makes this a cylindrical search through the mesh rather than a spherical one. Using centroids is fast, although the boundary changes slightly with mesh density.



Each element type has a different local face definition, so eTypeToFaceIndex maps every face to its local node indices. For the first three corner positions \(\mathbf{p}_0\), \(\mathbf{p}_1\), and \(\mathbf{p}_2\), the unit normal is
\[
\hat{\mathbf{n}}=
\frac{(\mathbf{p}_1-\mathbf{p}_0)\times(\mathbf{p}_2-\mathbf{p}_0)}
{\left\|(\mathbf{p}_1-\mathbf{p}_0)\times(\mathbf{p}_2-\mathbf{p}_0)\right\|}.
\]
The node order matters because reversing it reverses the normal. The face matches a target direction \(\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) when
\[
\left|\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{g}}-1\right|<10^{-3}.
\]
Because the test is near \(+1\), it accepts faces pointing with the target vector, not against it. The tolerance corresponds to roughly \(2.6^\circ\). The resulting element IDs and local face numbers can be assigned directly to a MeshElementFaces selection.
The final loop advances the search center in \(x\), creates one heat-flow object at each location, and gives each object a 2000 W peak at its matching time point. Mechanical interpolates between the tabular values, so additional points are needed if a square pulse is required.






NoteComplete script





import numpy as np

eTypeToFaceIndex = {
    ElementTypeEnum.kTri3: [[0, 1, 2]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTri6: [[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kQuad4: [[0, 1, 2, 4]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kQuad8: [[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTet4: [
        [0, 1, 3], [1, 2, 3], [2, 0, 3], [0, 2, 1]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTet10: [
        [0, 1, 3, 4, 8, 7],
        [1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 8],
        [2, 0, 3, 6, 7, 9],
        [0, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kPyramid5: [
        [0, 3, 2, 1], [0, 1, 4], [1, 2, 4], [3, 4, 2], [0, 4, 3]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kPyramid13: [
        [0, 3, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6, 5],
        [0, 1, 4, 5, 10, 9],
        [1, 2, 4, 6, 11, 10],
        [3, 4, 2, 12, 11, 7],
        [0, 4, 3, 9, 12, 8]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kWedge6: [
        [0, 2, 1], [3, 4, 5], [0, 1, 4, 3],
        [1, 2, 5, 4], [0, 3, 5, 2]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kWedge15: [
        [0, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6],
        [3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11],
        [0, 1, 4, 3, 6, 13, 9, 12],
        [1, 2, 5, 4, 7, 14, 10, 13],
        [0, 3, 5, 2, 12, 11, 14, 8]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kHex8: [
        [0, 1, 5, 4], [1, 2, 6, 5], [2, 3, 7, 6],
        [3, 0, 4, 7], [0, 3, 2, 1], [4, 5, 6, 7]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kHex20: [
        [0, 1, 5, 4, 8, 17, 12, 16],
        [1, 2, 6, 5, 9, 18, 13, 17],
        [2, 3, 7, 6, 10, 19, 14, 18],
        [3, 0, 4, 7, 11, 16, 15, 19],
        [0, 3, 2, 1, 11, 10, 9, 8],
        [4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15]
    ]
}

axeDict = {"xy": [0, 1], "xz": [0, 2], "yz": [1, 2]}


def highlight(selection):
    ExtAPI.SelectionManager.NewSelection(selection)


def getMeshData(ns, mesh):
    elementIds = []
    for geoId in ns.Location.Ids:
        elementIds.extend(mesh.MeshRegionById(geoId).ElementIds)

    elementIds = list(set(elementIds))
    elements = [mesh.ElementById(elementId) for elementId in elementIds]
    centroids = np.asarray(
        [list(element.Centroid) for element in elements],
        dtype=float
    )
    return elements, centroids


def getElementAroundCoords(meshData, coords, r, plane="xy"):
    elements, centroids = meshData
    coords = np.asarray(coords, dtype=float)
    axes = axeDict[plane]
    diffs = centroids[:, axes] - coords[axes]
    distSq = np.sum(diffs**2, axis=1)
    keep = distSq <= r**2
    return [element for element, include in zip(elements, keep) if include]


def findMatchingFaces(element, goalVector):
    goalVec = np.asarray(goalVector, dtype=float)
    goalLength = np.linalg.norm(goalVec)
    if goalLength == 0:
        raise ValueError("targetFaceVector cannot be zero")
    goalVec = goalVec / goalLength
    cornerNodes = element.CornerNodes
    matches = []

    for faceIndex, nodeIndices in enumerate(eTypeToFaceIndex[element.Type]):
        p0 = np.array([
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[0]].X,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[0]].Y,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[0]].Z
        ])
        p1 = np.array([
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[1]].X,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[1]].Y,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[1]].Z
        ])
        p2 = np.array([
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[2]].X,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[2]].Y,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[2]].Z
        ])

        normal = np.cross(p1 - p0, p2 - p0)
        normalLength = np.linalg.norm(normal)
        if normalLength == 0:
            continue
        normal = normal / normalLength
        if abs(np.dot(normal, goalVec) - 1) < 1e-3:
            matches.append(faceIndex)

    return matches


def elementsToFaces(elements, targetFaceVector):
    elementIds = []
    faceIndices = []

    for element in elements:
        matches = findMatchingFaces(element, targetFaceVector)
        if matches:
            elementIds.append(element.Id)
            faceIndices.append(matches[0])

    return elementIds, faceIndices


def createFaceSelection(elements, targetFaceVector):
    elementIds, faceIndices = elementsToFaces(elements, targetFaceVector)
    faceSelection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(
        SelectionTypeEnum.MeshElementFaces
    )
    faceSelection.Ids = elementIds
    faceSelection.ElementFaceIndices = faceIndices
    return faceSelection


def getFaceSelectionAtCoords(
    meshData, coords, r, targetFaceVector, plane="xy"
):
    elements = getElementAroundCoords(meshData, coords, r, plane)
    return createFaceSelection(elements, targetFaceVector)


def setHeatFlow(heatFlow, times, heats):
    heatFlow.Magnitude.Inputs[0].DiscreteValues = [
        Quantity(time, "s") for time in times
    ]
    heatFlow.Magnitude.Output.DiscreteValues = [
        Quantity(heat, "W") for heat in heats
    ]


globals().update(locals())

analysis = Model.Analyses[0]
meshData = getMeshData(
    Model.NamedSelections.Children[0],
    analysis.MeshData
)

nSteps = 10
deltaT = 1
coords = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
timeSteps = [step * deltaT for step in range(nSteps)]

settings = analysis.AnalysisSettings
settings.NumberOfSteps = 1
settings.CurrentStepNumber = 1
settings.StepEndTime = Quantity(nSteps * deltaT, "s")

for step in range(nSteps):
    faceSelection = getFaceSelectionAtCoords(
        meshData,
        coords,
        0.01,
        [0, 0, 1]
    )
    coords = coords + [0.015, 0, 0]

    heatFlow = analysis.AddHeatFlow()
    heatFlow.Name = "Custom Heat Flow " + str(step)
    heatFlow.Location = faceSelection

    heatValues = [
        2000 if timeIndex == step else 0
        for timeIndex in range(nSteps)
    ]
    setHeatFlow(heatFlow, timeSteps, heatValues)



Two guards are worth keeping: skip elements with no matching face, and reject zero-length target vectors or degenerate faces before normalizing them.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
from femmModel import Model

# Create an axisymmetric FEMM model
model = Model(radius=50, symetric=True)

# Load materials from FEMM's material library
air = model.loadMaterial("Air")
copper = model.loadMaterial("Copper")
iron = model.loadMaterial("Pure Iron")

# Create an air region
airBlock = model.addBlock(
    material=air,
    shape="rectangle",
    coords=[0, 0, 100, 100]
)

# Create an iron core
core = model.addBlock(
    material=iron,
    shape="rectangle",
    coords=[20, 0, 20, 50]
)

# Create a circular iron block
disk = model.addBlock(
    material=iron,
    shape="circle",
    coords=[40, 0, 10]
)

# Draw every block in the model
model.drawAll()

# Solve the FEMM model
model.solve()

# Get the force acting on the iron blocks
fx, fy = model.getForceOnBlocks([core, disk])

print("Force X:", fx)
print("Force Y:", fy)

# Get energy and co-energy for each block
energyTable = model.getEnergyTable()

print("\nEnergy Table:")
print(energyTable)

title: Checking Units
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Checking Units
One of the most tedious parts of automation in ANSYS is unit inconsistency. Rather than having to double check everything, I usually just use the below script as a mechanical snippet (the code is run every solve).
In a case where the same script is used across multiple projects, consider placing a unit checker at the top of your code.
# Accepted units: "m", "cm", "mm", or "um"
unit = "mm"

unitSystems = {
    "m": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardMKS,
    "cm": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardCGS,
    "mm": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardNMM,
    "um": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardUMKS
}

ExtAPI.Application.ActiveUnitSystem = unitSystems[unit]

print("Active unit system:", unit)

title: Creating Coordinate Systems From CSV
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Coordinate Systems From CSV
Often times clients will provide CSV files with information; in this case, I was given coordinate a table with coordinate systems’ locations and their names.
To accomplish this, I went through by row (ignoring the first), and edited the coordinate system object per iteration:
import csv

cs = Model.CoordinateSystems

file = '<PATH>'

with open(file, 'r') as csvF:
    reader = csv.reader(csvF)
    next(reader)
    
    for x in reader:
        newCS = cs.AddCoordinateSystem()
        newCS.Name = r"""""" + x[0] 
        newCS.OriginDefineBy = CoordinateSystemAlignmentType.Fixed
        
        newCS.OriginX = Quantity(float(x[1]), "m")
        newCS.OriginY = Quantity(float(x[2]), "m")
        newCS.OriginZ = Quantity(float(x[3]), "m")

text:
This is a technical source reference, not a finished blog post. It converts a 32-page slide presentation into readable Markdown, including information that was embedded in images and missed by PDF text extraction. Page numbers below refer to PDF pages, counting the title page as page 1. The accompanying slides/page-01.png through slides/page-32.png preserve all original figures; original-presentation.pdf preserves the source. Relative image links work when the complete folder is retained.
For a one-file workflow, this Markdown contains the principal content, equations, figure interpretations, and caveats. For maximum fidelity, use the complete folder and inspect the linked slide images when writing about a particular figure. This conversion is not a substitute for raw experimental data or a complete mathematical derivation. Approximate readings of plots are explicitly identified.

Title: A Survey of Passive Magnetic Springs
Event: 40th ASPE Annual Meeting, San Diego, California
Date printed on title slide: November 5, 2025



Author

Source footer websites: www.phyon.tech and pmc.mit.edu. These are transcribed source metadata, not independently verified references.



The presentation asks how to design useful passive magnetic springs with tractable formulas and modest computational effort before resorting to full 3D finite-element analysis (FEA). A central example is a long permanent magnet partly inserted into a soft magnetic tube. As overlap changes, cross-sectional regions with different magnetic energies replace one another. Their energy difference per unit length provides an approximate axial force.
This yields nearly constant force over a finite intermediate travel range. The force changes near the ends, and off-axis displacement can produce destabilizing lateral attraction. Iron improves force for a given magnet cross section but introduces saturation and hysteresis. Ironless layouts can recover comparable force by using larger magnets within a comparable overall envelope in the examples studied.
The presentation combines analytical magnetic circuits, 2D field calculations, 3D FEA comparisons, and a physical cylindrical-magnet experiment. The experiment’s 2D prediction is about 11 N; the measured plateau is roughly 10 N by visual reading. The reported hysteresis loop is about 60 mN, less than 1%. These are distinct observations, not a claim of less than 1% model error.

Page 1 contains the attribution above. Page 2 asks for useful design formulas addressing force, stiffness, travel, repeatability, low hysteresis, damping, parasitic forces and stiffness, temperature effects, and packaging. Design choices include magnet size, iron versus ironless constructions, Halbach arrangements, aspect ratio, and gap. A Linmot MagSpring product image illustrates an existing concept; it is not identified as the team’s prototype.
Page 3 lists gravity compensation (reduced energy consumption and actuator size), vibration isolation including quasi-zero-stiffness springs, and non-contact operation relevant to wear, friction, and cleanliness. Hysteresis and eddy currents remain possible damping mechanisms. Mechanical springs and pneumatics are alternatives.



Normal configurations change separation across facing surfaces; shear configurations change overlap through relative motion along the interacting surfaces. Torsional springs and actuators incorporating gravity compensation are also discussed. Variations include arrays, iron, ironless designs, and Halbach arrangements.
Modeling approaches: analytical magnet-pair formulas; equivalent magnetic charge or current; Fourier harmonic models; lumped magnetic circuits; 2D FEA (FEMM is identified by the presentation as free/open source); 3D FEA; and semi-analytical combinations.
Magnetic circuit analogy: reluctance corresponds to resistance, magnetomotive force (MMF) to voltage, and magnetic flux to current. Equivalent-charge/current illustration credited to Lahdo et al. 2017.



The figures contrast air/vacuum’s linear B-H response, soft iron’s nonlinear hysteresis loop, and a permanent magnet’s remanence and demagnetization curve. The magnet’s approximately linear recoil relation is:
B = B_r + mu*H
mu_r = mu/mu_0

title: Passive Magnetic Springs: Source Reference for a Blog Post
text:
The presentation asks how to design useful passive magnetic springs with tractable formulas and modest computational effort before resorting to full 3D finite-element analysis (FEA). A central example is a long permanent magnet partly inserted into a soft magnetic tube. As overlap changes, cross-sectional regions with different magnetic energies replace one another. Their energy difference per unit length provides an approximate axial force.
This yields nearly constant force over a finite intermediate travel range. The force changes near the ends, and off-axis displacement can produce destabilizing lateral attraction. Iron improves force for a given magnet cross section but introduces saturation and hysteresis. Ironless layouts can recover comparable force by using larger magnets within a comparable overall envelope in the examples studied.
The presentation combines analytical magnetic circuits, 2D field calculations, 3D FEA comparisons, and a physical cylindrical-magnet experiment. The experiment’s 2D prediction is about 11 N; the measured plateau is roughly 10 N by visual reading. The reported hysteresis loop is about 60 mN, less than 1%. These are distinct observations, not a claim of less than 1% model error.

Modeling approaches: analytical magnet-pair formulas; equivalent magnetic charge or current; Fourier harmonic models; lumped magnetic circuits; 2D FEA (FEMM is identified by the presentation as free/open source); 3D FEA; and semi-analytical combinations.
Magnetic circuit analogy: reluctance corresponds to resistance, magnetomotive force (MMF) to voltage, and magnetic flux to current. Equivalent-charge/current illustration credited to Lahdo et al. 2017.



The figures contrast air/vacuum’s linear B-H response, soft iron’s nonlinear hysteresis loop, and a permanent magnet’s remanence and demagnetization curve. The magnet’s approximately linear recoil relation is:
B = B_r + mu*H
mu_r = mu/mu_0
For air/vacuum, B = mu_0*H. For a general linear medium the relation is B = mu*H; the slide’s air/vacuum equation should not be generalized to every material. Page 7 shades magnetic energy areas on the B-H diagrams. These areas represent energy density (J/m^3), distinct from E_i (J/m).



Magnetic behavior depends on shape. A sourced illustration from www.mriquestions.com compares demagnetization factors for cylinders, plates, ellipsoids, a cube, and a sphere. A separate plot shows rectangular-section E_0/E* increasing from approximately 0.50 to 0.77 as w/t increases from 1 to 4 (visual readings, not tabulated data).
The slide prints B_0 = N B_ext but does not fully define the symbols or establish a general demagnetization law. Do not use that isolated expression as a universal design formula; the reliable takeaway here is shape dependence.



The rectangular magnet is poled across thickness t and moves axially into the tube. For a sufficiently long magnet and tube, the field can be approximated using three cross-sectional regions: empty tube, magnet inside tube, and magnet outside tube. The diagrams show magnetic-circuit and 2D field representations.
Define each E as magnetic energy per unit thickness of an axial slice. The approximate axial force magnitude for the indicated insertion direction is:
F ≈ E_0 - E_1
The circuit approximation for the air-gap flux density is:
B = B_r * (t/mu_r) / (t/mu_r + 2*g)
It treats the iron path as sufficiently permeable; saturated/thin iron requires a more complete calculation. E_0 can come from a handbook expression or 2D FEA. The normalization is:
E* = B_r^2 * t*w / (2*mu_r*mu_0)
The illustrated case gives E* = 101 J/m, E_1 = 0.09 E* = 9.1 J/m, and E_0 = 0.55 E* = 56 J/m. Their rounded difference is about 47 N, a derived estimate rather than an additional measurement.
Explanatory interpretation: if a displacement du replaces one slice with another, the energy changes by a quantity proportional to (E_0 - E_1)*du. Force follows from the change of energy with displacement. Do not insert an extra magnet length into the force equation: these E values are already per unit length.



Page 11 compares a nearly flat force estimate near F/E* ≈ 0.45 with a 3D FEA curve over insertion displacement. The numerical curve has entrance and exit effects. Agreement is best in the intermediate region; it is not uniform over all travel.
Page 12 shows that thinning the iron produces saturation and lowers the plateau (approximately 0.35 in the illustrated comparison). The same energy method can still be used, but E_1 should come from 2D FEA rather than the simple circuit formula. Field plots show localized high flux density.



For N52 magnets and 1018 steel in the studied rectangular configuration, a wall thickness about one-third of magnet width suffices. The graph plots F/E* against a/w for 2g/t = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3. Force increases with wall thickness and approaches a plateau; larger gaps lower force. This is a configuration-specific rule of thumb.



Lateral displacement attracts the magnet toward the tube wall. Negative stiffness is much larger parallel to the poling direction than transverse to it in this example. The example specifies an N52 magnet, a 1018 tube, w = 12 mm, t = 10 mm, and a = 6 mm.
The left plot gives lateral force per millimeter of insertion versus lateral offset. The right plot gives lateral negative stiffness per millimeter of insertion versus 2g/t. Do not quote these normalized plot values as the total device force or stiffness. Larger gaps reduce the destabilizing stiffness. A useful blog explanation is that nearly constant axial force does not imply lateral self-centering.



Splitting the cross section into a moving central piece and stationary side pieces reduces moving mass. In the depicted geometry, the central piece has thickness t/2 and the side pieces t/4 each. The energy expression becomes:
F = E_0 - (E_1 - E_2)
E_2 accounts for the remaining stationary assembly’s cross section, as shown in the diagrams. Reported rounded examples:

Page 19 overlays semi-analytical estimates and displacement-dependent 3D FEA curves for several constructions. Their plateaus differ; all show end effects. The original figure is the authority for curve-to-geometry mapping.
Page 20 specifies 2g/t = 0.1 (use this ratio rather than the slide’s looser verbal description of the gap). The drawing compares three approximately equal-force designs. This is a packaging comparison, not a claim that ironless designs always have identical size, mass, cost, or stiffness.



A diametrically poled cylindrical magnet is magnetized across its diameter, not along its length. For diameter d:
E* = pi*d^2*B_r^2 / (8*mu_r*mu_0)
E_0/E* = 1/2
F = E_0 - E_1
E_1/E* comes from 2D FEA. The normalized axial force falls as 2g/d increases. Page 22 gives the circular counterpart of the wall guideline: for N52 and 1018 steel, tube thickness about one-third of magnet diameter suffices in the studied cases. Curves shown are 2g/d = 0.1 and 0.25.



Lateral offset causes attraction toward the circular tube wall. Unlike the rectangular example, the presentation reports equal attraction for displacement in the poling and transverse directions. The left example uses a 6.35 mm magnet in an 8 mm-ID tube; the right varies tube ID for a 6.35 mm magnet. Forces and stiffness are normalized per millimeter of insertion. Increasing gap reduces negative stiffness.

Derived from the listed diameters, the radial clearance is (7 - 6.35)/2 = 0.325 mm, giving 2g/d ≈ 0.102. This arithmetic is added explanation, not an independent measurement.
The plot compares measurement (blue), 3D FEA (orange), and a constant 2D estimate (yellow dotted). Visually, measurement reaches roughly 10 N and gradually declines; 3D FEA reaches roughly 11 N and also rolls off near the end. Do not claim exact experimental agreement or report a numerical validation error from this plot without digitizing or obtaining raw data.



The iron tube exhibits some hysteresis. Cycling the magnet back and forth over several millimeters produces a force loop of about 60 mN, reported as less than 1%. The zoomed graph spans about 5-9 mm insertion and shows a change in force, not total axial force. Do not confuse the loop width with the simulation-to-measurement discrepancy.



The diagrams compare M1 and M2 magnet contributions, their sum, and an alternative M3 arrangement. A single magnet can provide nearly constant force over a moderate travel range. A coil can be packaged with the assembly to add active actuation; Choi et al. 2009 is cited as an example.
The plots use dimensionless force F/E* and displacement u in millimeters. Page 27’s M3 curve illustrates a comparatively flat positive-force region. The slides do not provide a full optimized actuator design or control implementation.



The model represents periodic magnet configurations using spatial harmonics. The iron backing is idealized with permeability tending to infinity. Two scalar-potential regions satisfy Laplace’s equation, ∇²ψ = 0. The moving permanent magnet is represented by magnetic charge density:
sigma_m(y, y_r) = sum_{k=1..infinity} [a_k(y_r)*cos(p*k*y) + b_k(y_r)*sin(p*k*y)]
p = 2*pi/lambda_u
Here y_r is relative displacement, lambda_u is the spatial period, k the harmonic number, D_f the out-of-plane depth, and H_y1(y,z_m1) the fixed-magnet-driven field intensity evaluated at z_m1. The slide prints:
F_m(y_r) = D_f * integral_0^lambda_u [sigma_m(y,y_r)*H_y1(y,z_m1)] dy

         = (mu_0*D_f*lambda_u/2) * sum_{k=1..infinity}
           a_k(y_r) * { [1-cosh(p*k*(z_2-z_s1))]*A_k
                        + sinh(p*k*(z_2-z_s1))*B_k }
                     / sinh(p*k*z_2)
This is a transcription, not an independently validated derivation. The slides do not fully define A_k, B_k, their boundary-condition calculation, or the magnetic-charge normalization. In particular, do not silently resolve unit conventions from the integral and expanded form without the underlying derivation. For a general blog, the harmonic concept and reported performance are more useful than presenting this as a ready-to-code solver.
The illustrated case labels a 20 mm period (lambda_pp on page 29), 5 mm magnet thicknesses, and a 0.5 mm gap. The plotted displacement response is approximately sinusoidal over 0-20 mm. Its vertical-axis labeling is not reliably readable, so do not quote an absolute force amplitude from it. The slide states that the first harmonic is accurate to within a few percent for the example; it does not establish this for every array.



The configuration is a coaxial pair magnetized along the axis. For tall magnets (t/R >> 1), the sticking/contact force approaches E* according to the slide. Reversing one magnet produces repulsion with nearly the same magnitude. The plot compares t/R = 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0; force decreases as separation increases.
The page does not restate the reference E* formula for this arrangement. The diagram labels R, while the axis uses u/r. Avoid building a numerical calculator from this slide without confirming radius and normalization conventions.



Three magnets with t/R = 0.5 form a push-pull arrangement: one interaction attracts while the other repels. The force-displacement curve is relatively flat near the middle of travel. The slide reports that small gaps and travels can attain F/E* ≈ 0.9. Plotted gap ratios are g/r = 0.2, 0.6, 1.0. The smallest gap yields the highest normalized force and a narrower available travel range. This is not a 90% energy efficiency claim.



The presentation concludes that E* provides an approximate upper-bound scale, changes in magnetic energy provide a useful route to force, and 2D FEA can exploit planar geometry and symmetry.
Listed next steps are design guidelines for stiffness and parasitic forces, misalignment, temperature variation, Halbach magnets, iron versus ironless designs, hysteresis estimates, and adding an actuator. These are future directions, not all completed results.

title: Creating RPs From NSs
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation - Remote Point Pairs from Named Selections
For this project, I needed to represent a six-degree-of-freedom spring between tracks (stationary) and rollers (dynamic). This approach used pairs of remote points that had translational/rotational constraints and whose initial position was determined by the average between the centroids.
If more pairs were required, it would definetly be worthwhile to replace the hardcoded filtering and function sequence with a dictionary that could be looped through.
def avgOfCentroids(nsList):
    pts = []
    x = y = z = 0

    for ns in nsList:
        for id in ns.Location.Ids:
            pts.append(ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(id).Centroid)

    for p in pts:
        x += p[0]
        y += p[1]
        z += p[2]
    return x/len(pts), y/len(pts), z/len(pts)

def createRPs(nsList):
    coords = avgOfCentroids(nsList)
    for ns in nsList:
        c = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()
        c.Name = ns.Name
        c.XCoordinate = Quantity(coords[0], "m")
        c.YCoordinate = Quantity(coords[1], "m")
        c.ZCoordinate = Quantity(coords[2], "m")
        c.PilotNodeAPDLName = ns.Name

        c.ScopingMethod = GeometryDefineByType.Component
        c.Location = ns

Ns = DataModel.GetObjectsByName("Named Selections")[0].Children

xRollers = [x for x in Ns if "xRoller" in x.Name]
zRollers = [x for x in Ns if "zRoller" in x.Name]
xSensors = [x for x in Ns if "xSensor" in x.Name]
zSensors = [x for x in Ns if "zSensor" in x.Name]
zSprings = [x for x in Ns if "ySpring" in x.Name]
thtaRollers = [x for x in Ns if "thRoller" in x.Name]

createRPs(xRollers)
createRPs(zRollers)
createRPs(xSensors)
createRPs(zSensors)
createRPs(zSprings)
createRPs(thtaRollers)

title: Automating 6DOF Bushing Contacts
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Creating 6DOF Bushing Contacts



Result of running script


When solving a mechanical model, points of contact can become extremely computationally demanding, requiring a heavily refined mesh around the contact region to determine local behavior. For some analyses, however, we do not require an accurate local representation and care more about the overall stiffness between two components.
In this case, we can simplify the expensive contact region with a 6 degree-of-freedom bushing joint, allowing us to represent the connection without the need for an extremely fine mesh.
The challenge to this approach is placing the bushing correctly. With the automation script I wrote below, all of the geometry difficulties are taken care of. The user must select 2 bodies (sphere + cylinder) and the script places a bushing contact lined up along the vector from the center of the sphere and cylinder.
(See end for notes about the code)
import numpy as np

_start_vars = set(dir())

def checkJ(cons):
    for x in cons:
        if "Joint" in str(x.ConnectionType):
            return x
    return None
    
def det3(M):
    return M[0][0]*(M[1][1]*M[2][2] - M[1][2]*M[2][1]) - M[0][1]*(M[1][0]*M[2][2] - M[1][2]*M[2][0]) + M[0][2]*(M[1][0]*M[2][1] - M[1][1]*M[2][0])

globals()['det3'] = det3

def solve_3x3(A, B):
    D = det3(A)
    Ax = [
        [B[0], A[0][1], A[0][2]],
        [B[1], A[1][1], A[1][2]],
        [B[2], A[2][1], A[2][2]]
    ]

    Ay = [
        [A[0][0], B[0], A[0][2]],
        [A[1][0], B[1], A[1][2]],
        [A[2][0], B[2], A[2][2]]
    ]

    Az = [
        [A[0][0], A[0][1], B[0]],
        [A[1][0], A[1][1], B[1]],
        [A[2][0], A[2][1], B[2]]
    ]

    return [det3(Ax)/D, det3(Ay)/D, det3(Az)/D]

globals()['solve_3x3'] = solve_3x3
    
def sphere_center(p1, p2, p3, p4):
    x1, y1, z1 = p1
    A = []
    B = []
    for x, y, z in [p2, p3, p4]:
        A.append([2*(x - x1), 2*(y - y1), 2*(z - z1)])
        B.append(x*x + y*y + z*z - x1*x1 - y1*y1 - z1*z1)

    return solve_3x3(A, B)



globals()['sphere_center'] = sphere_center

selected = list(ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CurrentSelection)

if "Sphere" in str(ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(selected[0]).SurfaceType):
    cylID = selected[1]
    sphereID = selected[0]
else:
    cylID = selected[0]
    sphereID = selected[1]

sph = ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(sphereID)
cyl = ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(cylID)

sphere = sph.Points
norms = cyl.Normals

norms = np.array(norms).reshape(-1, 3)
sphere = np.array(sphere).reshape(-1, 3)

p1 = norms[2]
p2 = norms[7]
p3 = norms[14]

A = np.vstack((p1, p2, p3))

eigenvalues, Vectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
D = np.diag(eigenvalues)

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(norms, full_matrices=True)
S = np.zeros((norms.shape[0], norms.shape[1]))
np.fill_diagonal(S, s)

dirCyl = np.array(Vt[2])

cs = Model.CoordinateSystems
cs1 = cs.AddCoordinateSystem()

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [cylID]

cs1.OriginLocation = selection

sphereCenter = np.array(sphere_center(sphere[0], sphere[10], sphere[20], sphere[30]))

cs1.PrimaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveZAxis
cs1.PrimaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(dirCyl[0], dirCyl[1], dirCyl[2])

pointOnCylAxis = np.array([
    float(str(cs1.OriginX).split(" ")[0]),
    float(str(cs1.OriginY).split(" ")[0]),
    float(str(cs1.OriginZ).split(" ")[0])
])

OP = np.array(pointOnCylAxis-sphereCenter)

AtoC = np.cross(np.cross(OP, dirCyl), dirCyl)

AtoC = AtoC / np.linalg.norm(AtoC)

actual_point = sphereCenter + sph.Radius*AtoC

cs1.OriginX = Quantity(str(actual_point[0]) + " [m]")
cs1.OriginY = Quantity(str(actual_point[1]) + " [m]")
cs1.OriginZ = Quantity(str(actual_point[2]) + " [m]")

cs1.PrimaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveZAxis
cs1.PrimaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(AtoC)

cs1.SecondaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveXAxis
cs1.SecondaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(dirCyl)

cons = Model.Connections.Children

group = checkJ(cons)

if checkJ(cons) is None:
    group = Model.Connections.AddConnectionGroup()

group.ConnectionType = AutoDetectionType.Joint

joint = group.AddJoint()
joint.Type = JointType.Bushing

rp1 = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()
rp2 = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [cylID]

rp1.Location = selection

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [sphereID]

rp2.Location = selection

joint.ReferenceLocation = rp1
joint.MobileLocation = rp2

rp1.CoordinateSystem = cs2
rp2.CoordinateSystem = cs2

When it came to finding the center of the sphere, I recycled it from one of my older scripts before found out how to use CPython (numpy) in ansys mechanical so there are multiple technically not needed functions above that do smaller scale matrix operations.
Because CPython is still technically in beta, there are many weird bugs when it comes to compiling these scripts. In this code specifically, I had to force various functions to be considered global so I could access them at all using globals()['sphere_center'] = sphere_center.
If this code were to be used for a large amount of connections, I would recommend writing a function which sorts your selections into pairs based on centroid proximity and looping through these pairs with the above code.

title: Designing Passive Magnetic Springs with Energy-Based Models
text:
A vertical actuator should not have to spend energy continuously just to hold up a payload. A passive spring can carry that static load, leaving the actuator to handle motion and disturbance rejection. Conventional springs can do this, but their force usually changes with displacement. A well-designed magnetic spring can instead provide a nearly constant force over a useful range of travel, without contact between its moving parts.
By utilizing the difference in magnetic energy between two cross sections, force may be estimated. That produces a useful design model before the expense of a full three-dimensional finite-element analysis (FEA). We then test the approach against 3D simulations and a physical cylindrical-magnet experiment.


A magnetic spring is not useful merely because two magnets attract or repel. Its force-displacement curve must suit the mechanism around it. For gravity compensation, the desired behavior is often a force that changes very little across the operating stroke.
The presentation surveys several ways to create that behavior: normal-force arrangements, shear arrangements, iron-backed and ironless designs, magnet arrays, and push-pull configurations. It also highlights the quantities that a force-only design can miss: lateral stiffness, hysteresis, damping, temperature sensitivity, moving mass, and package size.
The clearest example is a long permanent magnet that slides axially into a soft-magnetic tube. The magnet is polarized across its cross section, so this is a shear configuration: axial motion changes the overlap between magnet and tube without changing the radial air gap.






Figure 1: A long transversely poled magnet entering a soft-magnetic tube can be divided into nearly two-dimensional cross-sectional regions. The field plots and magnetic-circuit analogy are analytical and simulation tools, not measurements. Source: Verdirame et al., presentation slide 9.



If the magnet and tube are sufficiently long, most of the device can be represented by three cross sections: an empty tube, a magnet inside the tube, and a magnet outside the tube. Only the entrance and exit are strongly three-dimensional. This separation is what makes the energy method practical.



Let (E_0) be the magnetic energy per unit axial length of the magnet outside the tube, and let (E_1) be the corresponding energy per unit length with the magnet inside the tube. Both have units of joules per meter, which is dimensionally equivalent to newtons.
As the magnet advances by a small distance (du), one cross-sectional slice changes from the outside state to the inside state. The presentation therefore estimates the axial force magnitude as
\[
F \approx E_0-E_1.
\]
A useful interpretation is to write the total magnetic energy as a sum of the two regions. Increasing the overlap transfers length from the (E_0) region to the (E_1) region, so differentiating energy with respect to displacement produces their difference. No extra magnet length belongs in the force equation because each (E_i) is already an energy per unit length.
For the rectangular tube model, the air-gap flux density is approximated with a magnetic circuit:
\[
B = B_r\frac{t/\mu_r}{t/\mu_r+2g},
\]
where (B_r) is the magnet remanence, (t) is its dimension along the poling direction, (g) is the one-sided air gap, and (mu_r) is the magnet recoil relative permeability. This relation assumes that the iron provides a sufficiently permeable return path. Thin or saturated iron violates that simplifying assumption.
The presentation normalizes results by the reference energy per unit length
\[
E^*=\frac{B_r^2tw}{2\mu_r\mu_0},
\]
where (w) is the other cross-sectional dimension and (mu_0) is the permeability of free space. For the illustrated rectangular example, the stated values are (E^=101 ), (E_0=0.55E^=56 ), and (E_1=0.09E^*=9.1 ). Their rounded difference gives an estimated force of about (47 ). It is not an experimental result.



The cross-sectional estimate has no entrance or exit, so it predicts a constant force. A 3D model restores those end effects.






Figure 2: The dotted line is the energy-based estimate; the solid curve is 3D FEA. Agreement is strongest after entry and before the far end of the tube. Source: Verdirame et al., presentation slide 11.



In the simulated curve, force rises as the magnet enters the tube, stays near (0.45E^*) across an intermediate region, and then falls as the magnet approaches the other end. The analytical estimate is therefore most useful for sizing the plateau force. Travel limits and end behavior still need a 3D calculation or a measurement.
The same division of labor applies to the iron. If the wall is thick enough to remain below strong saturation, a magnetic circuit provides a quick estimate of (E_1). If the wall is too thin, local saturation increases the energy of the inside state and reduces the plateau force. The presentation recommends obtaining (E_1) from 2D FEA in that case.
For the studied N52 magnet and 1018-steel rectangular geometry, the simulated force approaches a plateau once the wall thickness is about one-third of the magnet width. Larger air gaps reduce force. That one-third value is a configuration-specific sizing observation, not a universal rule for other steels, magnet grades, or geometries.



Soft iron concentrates flux and increases force for a given magnet cross section, but it also brings saturation and hysteresis. An ironless design removes that major hysteretic material at the cost of more magnet volume for the same force.






Figure 3: The presentation’s equal-force packaging comparison. In the stated geometry, the iron-backed design reaches about (0.45E^), while the three-magnet ironless arrangement reaches about (0.15E^) for the same magnet-area normalization. Source: Verdirame et al., presentation slide 20.



For the particular comparison shown, with (2g/t=0.1) and iron wall thickness (a=w/3), the iron-backed design produces approximately (0.45E^). A three-magnet ironless layout produces approximately (0.15E^) when normalized by the same total magnet area. Because (E^*) scales with magnet cross-sectional area, about three times the magnet area can recover similar force. If both linear dimensions are scaled together, that corresponds to a factor of (sqrt{3}).
This is a packaging tradeoff, not a general claim that the alternatives have identical mass, cost, thermal behavior, or lateral stiffness. The design choice depends on whether compactness or low hysteresis matters more.



The physical test used a diametrically poled N52 cylindrical magnet: its magnetization points across the diameter rather than along its axis. The magnet was 6.35 mm in diameter and 25.4 mm long. It moved into a 25 mm-long 1018-steel tube with a 7 mm inner diameter and a 16 mm outer diameter.
For a circular magnet of diameter (d), the presentation uses
\[
E^*=\frac{\pi d^2B_r^2}{8\mu_r\mu_0}, \qquad \frac{E_0}{E^*}=\frac{1}{2},
\]
and obtains (E_1/E^) from 2D FEA. The reported reference scale for the test magnet is (E^ ). The diameters imply a radial clearance of
\[
g=\frac{7-6.35}{2}=0.325\ \mathrm{mm},
\]
so (2g/d). This ratio is arithmetic derived from the stated dimensions, not a separate measurement.

The measurement confirms the intended order of magnitude and the existence of a broad force plateau. The plot does not provide raw data or uncertainty bounds, so it does not support an exact model-error percentage. The reported “less than 1%” refers to the measured hysteresis loop, not to agreement between simulation and experiment.






Figure 5: Repeated motion over part of the stroke produced a measured force loop of about 60 mN. The enlarged graph shows change in force, not the full axial force. Source: Verdirame et al., presentation slide 25.






The tube attracts an off-center magnet toward the nearest wall. That is a negative lateral stiffness: a small radial displacement produces a force that increases the displacement instead of restoring the magnet to center.






Figure 6: Two-dimensional FEA of the cylindrical case shows lateral attraction and predicts lower negative stiffness as the radial gap increases. The plotted quantities are normalized per millimeter of insertion. Source: Verdirame et al., presentation slide 23.



In the circular example, the presentation reports the same attraction for offsets parallel and transverse to the poling direction. Increasing the air gap reduces this destabilizing stiffness, but also reduces axial force. Bearings, flexures, or another guidance mechanism must therefore react the lateral load. A nearly flat axial force curve should never be interpreted as self-centering behavior.



The work establishes a compact route from magnetic energy to preliminary spring sizing and demonstrates it on one cylindrical prototype. It does not claim perfectly constant force, zero hysteresis, stability in every direction, or universal wall-thickness rules.
The presentation identifies misalignment, temperature variation, parasitic stiffness, Halbach arrangements, hysteresis prediction, and actuator integration as continuing work. Those are exactly the issues that separate a promising force curve from a complete gravity-compensation mechanism.
